AverageLMC/Assumptions.lean.title: Coordinate smoothness constants of the potential
AverageLMC/Assumptions.lean.summary:
This section fixes the objects in terms of which every later estimate is stated. The state space is \(\mathbb R^p\) with the Euclidean inner product \(\langle x,y angle=\sum_{j=1}^px_jy_j\), the norm \(\|x\|=\langle x,x angle^{1/2}\) and the canonical basis \(e_1,\dots,e_p\). The potential is a function \(f:\mathbb R^p o\mathbb R\) with gradient \( abla f\) and partial derivatives \(\partial_jf(x)=\langle abla f(x),e_j angle\). Following the notation section of the paper, the coordinate smoothness constants, their average and the global smoothness constant are

\[ egin{aligned} M_j&=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^p,\ a e0} rac{2 igl(f(x+ae_j)-f(x)-a\,\partial_jf(x) igr)}{a^2},\ M_{ m av}&= rac1p\sum_{j=1}^pM_j,\ M_\infty&=\sup_{x e y} rac{\| abla f(x)- abla f(y)\|}{\|x-y\|}. \end{aligned}\]

All three are computed from the potential itself; they are not additional parameters. For a differentiable \(f\) whose gradient is \(M\)-Lipschitz we prove that both suprema are finite, that \( abla f\) is \(M_\infty\)-Lipschitz, and that the coordinate quadratic upper model \(f(x+ae_j)\le f(x)+a\,\partial_jf(x)+ frac12M_ja^2\) holds. If in addition \(f\) is \(m\)-strongly convex, then \(m\le M_j\le M_\infty\) for every \(j\) and \(m\le M_{ m av}\le M_\infty\). No second derivative is used for these facts.

The section also defines the Hessian matrix \( abla^2f(x)\), the Laplacian \(\Delta f(x)\), the third-order condition of the paper's Section 4, \(\sup_x\| abla\Delta f(x)\|^2\le M_\Delta^2p\) for a three times continuously differentiable potential, and the root-mean-square constant \(M_{ m rms}\) for a finite sum of potentials, and it proves \(\operatorname{tr} abla^2f=\Delta f\). The coordinate upper model is the input of the Gaussian smoothing lemma, the comparisons between \(m\), \(M_{ m av}\) and \(M_\infty\) are used when the one-step bounds are iterated, and the remaining definitions enter the Laplacian-smooth theorem and the stochastic-gradient theorem.

steps.title: Coordinates and coordinate Taylor quotients
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(p\in\mathbb N\). Write \(e_j\in\mathbb R^p\) for the vector whose \(j\)th coordinate is \(1\) and whose other coordinates are \(0\). For a function \(f:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) the gradient \(\nabla f(x)\) is the vector representing the derivative, \(Df(x)v=\langle\nabla f(x),v\rangle\) for all \(v\), and \(\partial_jf(x)\) is its \(j\)th coordinate. For \(x\in\mathbb R^p\) and a real number \(a\ne0\) the coordinate Taylor quotient is

\[Q_j(x,a)=\frac{2\bigl(f(x+ae_j)-f(x)-a\,\partial_jf(x)\bigr)}{a^2},\]

that is, twice the error of the first-order approximation of \(f\) along the \(j\)th coordinate line, divided by the squared displacement. Let \(\mathcal Q_j=\{Q_j(x,a):x\in\mathbb R^p,\ a\in\mathbb R,\ a\ne0\}\). The coordinate smoothness constant is \(M_j=\sup\mathcal Q_j\), and for \(p\ge1\) the average smoothness constant is \(M_{\rm av}=\frac1p\sum_{j=1}^pM_j\). The supremum of a nonempty set of real numbers is a real number exactly when the set is bounded above; Step 3 shows that \(\mathcal Q_j\) is bounded above whenever \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz, and \(M_j\) is used only under that hypothesis.

Claim. For every \(f\), every \(j\in\{1,\dots,p\}\) and every \(x\in\mathbb R^p\):

  1. the set \(\mathcal Q_j\) is nonempty;
  2. \(\|e_j\|=1\);
  3. \(\langle x,e_j\rangle=x_j\). In particular \(\langle\nabla f(x),e_j\rangle=\partial_jf(x)\).

Proof. (1) The number \(Q_j(0,1)\) is obtained from the admissible choice \(x=0\), \(a=1\ne0\), so it belongs to \(\mathcal Q_j\). (2) The only nonzero coordinate of \(e_j\) equals \(1\), so \(\|e_j\|^2=\sum_i(e_j)_i^2=1\) and \(\|e_j\|=1\). (3) By definition of the inner product, \(\langle x,e_j\rangle=\sum_ix_i(e_j)_i=x_j\), since \((e_j)_i=0\) for \(i\ne j\) and \((e_j)_j=1\). Applying this with \(x\) replaced by \(\nabla f(x)\) gives the last assertion. \(\square\)

Identities (2) and (3) are used to evaluate the inner product and the norm of a coordinate displacement \(ae_j\): \(\langle v,ae_j\rangle=a\,v_j\) and \(\|ae_j\|^2=a^2\).

steps.title: The Lipschitz seminorm of the gradient
steps.body:
Definition. For \(f:\mathbb R^p o\mathbb R\) let \(\mathcal G= igl\{\| abla f(x)- abla f(y)\|/\|x-y\|:x,y\in\mathbb R^p,\ x e y igr\}\) and \(M_\infty=\sup\mathcal G\), the Lipschitz seminorm of the gradient. A number \(M\ge0\) is a Lipschitz constant of \( abla f\) if \(\| abla f(x)- abla f(y)\|\le M\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\).

Claim. Let \(p\ge1\), and let \( abla f\) be Lipschitz with some constant \(M\ge0\). Then

  1. \(M_\infty\le M\);
  2. \(M_\infty\ge0\);
  3. \( abla f\) is Lipschitz with constant \(M_\infty\): \(\| abla f(x)- abla f(y)\|\le M_\infty\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^p\).

Thus \(M_\infty\) is the smallest Lipschitz constant of \( abla f\), and later estimates may be stated with this exact constant.

Proof. The set \(\mathcal G\) is nonempty. Since \(p\ge1\), the vector \(e_1\) exists, and \(e_1 e0\) because \(\|e_1\|=1 e0=\|0\|\). Hence the quotient at the pair \((0,e_1)\) belongs to \(\mathcal G\).

\(M\) is an upper bound of \(\mathcal G\). If \(x e y\), then \(\|x-y\|>0\), and dividing the Lipschitz inequality \(\| abla f(x)- abla f(y)\|\le M\|x-y\|\) by \(\|x-y\|\) gives \(\| abla f(x)- abla f(y)\|/\|x-y\|\le M\).

(1) A nonempty set of reals with an upper bound has a least upper bound, and the least upper bound is at most every upper bound; hence \(M_\infty\le M\).

(2) Every element of \(\mathcal G\) is a quotient of two nonnegative numbers, hence nonnegative. The element at \((0,e_1)\) is therefore \(\ge0\), and it is \(\le M_\infty\) because \(M_\infty\) is an upper bound of \(\mathcal G\).

(3) If \(x=y\), both sides of the inequality are \(0\). If \(x e y\), the quotient at \((x,y)\) belongs to \(\mathcal G\), so \(\| abla f(x)- abla f(y)\|/\|x-y\|\le M_\infty\); multiplying by \(\|x-y\|>0\) gives the inequality. \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(p\ge1\) is used only to produce an element of \(\mathcal G\): for \(p=0\) the space is \(\{0\}\), \(\mathcal G\) is empty and its supremum is not defined.

steps.title: The coordinate quadratic upper model
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(f:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and let \(\nabla f\) be Lipschitz with constant \(M\ge0\). Then for every \(j\):

  1. \(Q_j(x,a)\le M\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^p\) and every \(a\ne0\);
  2. \(\mathcal Q_j\) is bounded above, so \(M_j=\sup\mathcal Q_j\) is a real number, and \(M_j\le M\);
  3. for every \(x\in\mathbb R^p\) and every \(a\in\mathbb R\), including \(a=0\), \[f(x+ae_j)\le f(x)+a\,\partial_jf(x)+\frac{M_j}{2}\,a^2.\qquad(1)\]

Proof. We use the descent inequality: for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^p\),

\[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac M2\|y-x\|^2.\qquad(2)\]

To recall its proof, put \(d=y-x\) and \(g(t)=f(x+td)\) for \(t\in[0,1]\). By the chain rule \(g'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+td),d\rangle\), which is continuous in \(t\) because \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the Lipschitz bound,

\[f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle=\int_0^1\langle\nabla f(x+td)-\nabla f(x),d\rangle\,dt\le\int_0^1Mt\|d\|^2\,dt=\frac M2\|d\|^2.\]

(1) Fix \(x\) and \(a\ne0\), and apply (2) with \(y=x+ae_j\). Then \(y-x=ae_j\), \(\langle\nabla f(x),ae_j\rangle=a\,\partial_jf(x)\) and \(\|ae_j\|^2=a^2\|e_j\|^2=a^2\) by Step 1. Hence

\[f(x+ae_j)-f(x)-a\,\partial_jf(x)\le\frac M2\,a^2.\]

Multiplying by \(2\) and dividing by \(a^2>0\) gives \(Q_j(x,a)\le M\).

(2) By (1), \(M\) is an upper bound of \(\mathcal Q_j\). The set is nonempty by Step 1, so its supremum \(M_j\) exists and is at most the upper bound \(M\).

(3) If \(a=0\), both sides of (1) equal \(f(x)\). If \(a\ne0\), then \(Q_j(x,a)\in\mathcal Q_j\), so \(Q_j(x,a)\le M_j\) by definition of the supremum (which exists by (2)). Multiplying this inequality by \(a^2/2>0\) gives \(f(x+ae_j)-f(x)-a\,\partial_jf(x)\le\frac{M_j}2a^2\), which is (1). \(\square\)

Inequality (1) has the coefficient \(M_j/2\) in place of the coefficient \(M/2\) given by (2) along the line \(x+\mathbb Re_j\); the two can differ substantially when the potential is much stiffer in some directions than along the coordinate axes. Only differentiability and a Lipschitz gradient are used; the existence of second derivatives is not needed.

steps.title: Comparison of strong convexity, average smoothness and global smoothness
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(f:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(M\ge0\).

  1. If \(f\) is \(m\)-strongly convex for some \(m\in\mathbb R\), then \(m\le M_j\) for every \(j\).
  2. If \(p\ge1\), then \(M_{\rm av}\le M\).
  3. If \(p\ge1\), then \(M_j\le M_\infty\) for every \(j\), and \(M_{\rm av}\le M_\infty\).
  4. If \(p\ge1\) and \(f\) is \(m\)-strongly convex, then \(m\le M_{\rm av}\).

Consequently, for \(p\ge1\) and an \(m\)-strongly convex \(f\), \(m\le M_{\rm av}\le M_\infty\le M\).

Here \(f\) is \(m\)-strongly convex if \(f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)-\frac m2t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(t\in[0,1]\).

Proof. (1) For a differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex function the supporting-plane inequality holds:

\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac m2\|y-x\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y.\qquad(3)\]

To recall why, note that \(g(v)=f(v)-\frac m2\|v\|^2\) is convex: inserting the identity \(\|(1-t)x+ty\|^2=(1-t)\|x\|^2+t\|y\|^2-t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2\) into the definition of strong convexity gives exactly the convexity inequality for \(g\). A differentiable convex function lies above its tangent planes, \(g(y)\ge g(x)+Dg(x)(y-x)\), and \(Dg(x)v=\langle\nabla f(x),v\rangle-m\langle x,v\rangle\). Since \(\|y\|^2-\|x\|^2-2\langle x,y-x\rangle=\|y-x\|^2\), this tangent-plane inequality is (3).

Apply (3) with \(x=0\) and \(y=e_j\), and apply the coordinate upper model (1) of Step 3 with \(x=0\) and \(a=1\). Using \(\langle\nabla f(0),e_j\rangle=\partial_jf(0)\) and \(\|e_j\|=1\),

\[f(0)+\partial_jf(0)+\frac m2\le f(e_j)\le f(0)+\partial_jf(0)+\frac{M_j}2.\]

Cancelling \(f(0)+\partial_jf(0)\) and multiplying by \(2\) gives \(m\le M_j\).

(2) By Step 3, \(M_j\le M\) for each of the \(p\) indices. Summing, \(\sum_jM_j\le pM\), and dividing by \(p>0\) gives \(M_{\rm av}\le M\).

(3) By Step 2, \(M_\infty\ge0\) and \(\nabla f\) is \(M_\infty\)-Lipschitz. Applying Step 3 and part (2) with the Lipschitz constant \(M_\infty\) in place of \(M\) gives \(M_j\le M_\infty\) and \(M_{\rm av}\le M_\infty\).

(4) Summing (1) over \(j\) gives \(pm\le\sum_jM_j\), and dividing by \(p>0\) gives \(m\le M_{\rm av}\). The final chain combines (4), (3) and Step 2. \(\square\)

The constants \(M_j\), \(M_{\rm av}\) and \(M_\infty\) in these inequalities are the suprema defined from \(f\), not arbitrary upper bounds; this is what allows the later theorems to be stated with the constants of the paper. The inequality \(m\le M_{\rm av}\) is used, for example, to guarantee \(mh\le1\) when \(hM_\infty\le1\).

steps.title: Hessian, Laplacian and the constants of the third-order and finite-sum settings
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(D^2f(x)\) denote the second derivative of \(f\) at \(x\), a bilinear form on \(\mathbb R^p\) (as usual for derivatives defined at every point, it is taken to be \(0\) where it does not exist).

  • The Hessian matrix is \(\nabla^2f(x)=\bigl(D^2f(x)(e_i,e_j)\bigr)_{i,j=1}^p\).
  • The Laplacian is the trace of \(D^2f(x)\) with respect to the inner product: \(\Delta f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^pD^2f(x)(v_i,v_i)\) for an orthonormal basis \(v_1,\dots,v_p\). The sum does not depend on the orthonormal basis, because a change of orthonormal basis is given by an orthogonal matrix \(O\) and \(\sum_iD^2f(x)(Ov_i,Ov_i)=\operatorname{tr}(O^\top AO)=\operatorname{tr}A\) for the matrix \(A\) of \(D^2f(x)\).
  • For \(M_\Delta\in\mathbb R\), the potential satisfies the Laplacian smoothness condition if \(f\) is three times continuously differentiable and \(\|\nabla\Delta f(x)\|^2\le M_\Delta^2\,p\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^p\). No Lipschitz condition on the Hessian is part of this condition.
  • For a finite family \(f_1,\dots,f_n:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\), let \(M_\infty(f_i)\) be the gradient seminorm of Step 2 for \(f_i\). The root-mean-square component smoothness is \(M_{\rm rms}=\bigl(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nM_\infty(f_i)^2\bigr)^{1/2}\).

Claim. For every \(f:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) and every \(x\in\mathbb R^p\), \(\operatorname{tr}\nabla^2f(x)=\Delta f(x)\).

Proof. The canonical basis \(e_1,\dots,e_p\) is orthonormal, so by the definition of the Laplacian with \(v_i=e_i\),

\[\Delta f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^pD^2f(x)(e_i,e_i)=\sum_{i=1}^p\bigl(\nabla^2f(x)\bigr)_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}\nabla^2f(x).\qquad\square\]

AverageLMC/GradientStep.lean.title: The gradient-step and descent inequalities
AverageLMC/GradientStep.lean.summary:
This section proves the two deterministic inequalities used in the proof of Theorem 1. They concern one gradient step \( heta\mapsto heta-h abla f( heta)\) with step \(h\ge0\) for a differentiable potential \(f\) on a real Hilbert space \(H\) (in the applications \(H=\mathbb R^p\)). The first, the gradient-step lemma (eq:basic-gd) of the paper, uses \(m\)-strong convexity:

\[\| heta-h abla f( heta)-y\|^2\le(1-mh)\| heta-y\|^2+2h igl(f(y)-f( heta) igr)+h^2\| abla f( heta)\|^2\qquad( heta,y\in H).\]

The second, the deterministic half (eq:exp-upper) of the smoothing lemma, uses an \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient:

\[2 igl(f( heta-h abla f( heta))-f( heta) igr)\le-h(2-hM)\| abla f( heta)\|^2.\]

In the proof of Theorem 1 the first inequality is applied with \( heta=\vartheta\) and \(y=Y\), where \(Y\sim\pi\) is coupled with the current iterate \(\vartheta\); the second controls the potential after the gradient step. When the two are added, the potential values cancel and the coefficient \(h^2(hM-1)\) of \(\| abla f(\vartheta)\|^2\) remains.

steps.title: The gradient-step lemma
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex for some \(m\in\mathbb R\), and let \(h\ge0\). Then for all \(\theta,y\in H\),

\[\|\theta-h\nabla f(\theta)-y\|^2\le(1-mh)\|\theta-y\|^2+2h\bigl(f(y)-f(\theta)\bigr)+h^2\|\nabla f(\theta)\|^2.\]

Proof. Write \(g=\nabla f(\theta)\) and \(d=\theta-y\). Since \(\theta-hg-y=d-hg\), expanding the square of the norm with \(\|u-v\|^2=\|u\|^2-2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\) and \(\|hg\|=|h|\,\|g\|=h\|g\|\) gives

\[\|\theta-hg-y\|^2=\|d\|^2-2h\langle d,g\rangle+h^2\|g\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

The supporting-plane inequality of a differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex function (inequality (3) of the previous section, valid in every real Hilbert space) at the base point \(\theta\) and the point \(y\) reads

\[f(\theta)+\langle g,y-\theta\rangle+\frac m2\|y-\theta\|^2\le f(y).\]

Since \(y-\theta=-d\), we have \(\langle g,y-\theta\rangle=-\langle d,g\rangle\) and \(\|y-\theta\|=\|d\|\), so the inequality becomes

\[-\langle d,g\rangle\le f(y)-f(\theta)-\frac m2\|d\|^2.\qquad(2)\]

Multiplying (2) by the nonnegative number \(2h\) preserves the inequality: \(-2h\langle d,g\rangle\le2h(f(y)-f(\theta))-mh\|d\|^2\). Substituting this bound into (1),

\[\|\theta-hg-y\|^2\le\|d\|^2-mh\|d\|^2+2h\bigl(f(y)-f(\theta)\bigr)+h^2\|g\|^2,\]

which is the claim, since \(\|d\|^2-mh\|d\|^2=(1-mh)\|\theta-y\|^2\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(h\ge0\) is used twice: to write \(\|hg\|=h\|g\|\) and to multiply (2) by \(2h\). For \(h=0\) the claim reduces to \(\|\theta-y\|^2\le\|\theta-y\|^2\). No sign condition on \(m\) and no smoothness of \(\nabla f\) are needed.

steps.title: Descent of the potential along a gradient step
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(M\ge0\), and let \(\theta\in H\) and \(h\ge0\). Then

\[2\bigl(f(\theta-h\nabla f(\theta))-f(\theta)\bigr)\le-h(2-hM)\|\nabla f(\theta)\|^2.\qquad(3)\]

If moreover \(hM\le2\), then \(f(\theta-h\nabla f(\theta))\le f(\theta)\).

Proof. Write \(g=\nabla f(\theta)\). The descent inequality \(f(z)\le f(\theta)+\langle g,z-\theta\rangle+\frac M2\|z-\theta\|^2\), proved in the previous section from the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment from \(\theta\) to \(z\), applies to \(z=\theta-hg\). There \(z-\theta=-hg\), so \(\langle g,z-\theta\rangle=-h\langle g,g\rangle=-h\|g\|^2\) and \(\|z-\theta\|^2=|-h|^2\|g\|^2=h^2\|g\|^2\). Hence

\[f(\theta-hg)\le f(\theta)-h\|g\|^2+\frac M2h^2\|g\|^2.\]

Subtracting \(f(\theta)\) and multiplying by \(2\),

\[2\bigl(f(\theta-hg)-f(\theta)\bigr)\le-2h\|g\|^2+Mh^2\|g\|^2=-h(2-hM)\|g\|^2,\]

which is (3). If \(hM\le2\), the three factors \(-h\le0\), \(2-hM\ge0\) and \(\|g\|^2\ge0\) make the right-hand side of (3) a product of a nonpositive and two nonnegative numbers, hence \(\le0\). Therefore \(2(f(\theta-hg)-f(\theta))\le0\), which is the second assertion. \(\square\)

In Theorem 1 the step satisfies \(hM_\infty\le1\), so the second assertion applies: the gradient step does not increase the potential. Only (3) itself enters the one-step bound, where its right-hand side combines with the term \(h^2\|\nabla f(\vartheta)\|^2\) of the gradient-step lemma.

steps.title: The contraction factor is at most an exponential
steps.body:
Claim. For every real \(t\) with \(0\le t\le1\),

\[\frac{1-t}{1+t}\le e^{-2t}.\]

Proof. If \(t=1\), the left-hand side is \(0\) and the right-hand side \(e^{-2}\) is positive. Let \(0\le t<1\), so that \(1+t>0\) and \(1-t>0\). Consider \(\varphi(s)=\log(1+s)-\log(1-s)-2s\) on \([0,1)\). Then \(\varphi(0)=0\) and

\[\varphi'(s)=\frac1{1+s}+\frac1{1-s}-2=\frac{2}{1-s^2}-2=\frac{2s^2}{1-s^2}\ge0,\]

so \(\varphi\) is nondecreasing by the mean value theorem and \(\varphi(t)\ge0\), that is,

\[2t\le\log\frac{1+t}{1-t}.\qquad(1)\]

(Equivalently, \(t\) is the first term of the series \(\frac12\log\frac{1+t}{1-t}=\sum_{i\ge0}\frac{t^{2i+1}}{2i+1}\), whose terms are nonnegative.) Since \(\frac{1-t}{1+t}=\bigl(\frac{1+t}{1-t}\bigr)^{-1}\) and \(\log(x^{-1})=-\log x\) for \(x>0\), (1) gives \(\log\frac{1-t}{1+t}\le-2t\). The exponential is increasing and \(\frac{1-t}{1+t}>0\), so exponentiating gives the claim. \(\square\)

In the applications \(t=mh\), and \(t\le1\) follows from \(m\le M_\infty\) and \(hM_\infty\le1\).

steps.title: Iterating an affine inequality over a finite horizon
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((r_k)_{k\ge0}\) be real numbers, let \(q\ge0\), \(c\ge0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\), and suppose that

\[r_{j+1}\le q\,r_j+(1-q)\,c\qquad\text{for every }j<n.\]

Then \(r_n\le q^nr_0+c\).

Proof. We first prove by induction on \(k\) that

\[r_k\le q^kr_0+(1-q^k)\,c\qquad\text{for every }k\le n.\qquad(2)\]

Base case \(k=0\). Since \(q^0=1\), the right-hand side is \(r_0\).

Inductive step. Let \(k+1\le n\) and assume (2) for \(k\) (which is allowed since \(k\le n\)). Because \(q\ge0\), multiplying the induction hypothesis by \(q\) preserves it: \(q\,r_k\le q^{k+1}r_0+(q-q^{k+1})c\). Since \(k<n\), the hypothesis applies with \(j=k\):

\[r_{k+1}\le q\,r_k+(1-q)c\le q^{k+1}r_0+(q-q^{k+1}+1-q)\,c=q^{k+1}r_0+(1-q^{k+1})\,c.\]

This proves (2). For \(k=n\), (2) gives \(r_n\le q^nr_0+c-q^nc\le q^nr_0+c\), because \(q^nc\ge0\) as a product of the nonnegative numbers \(q^n\) and \(c\). \(\square\)

The constant \(c\) is the fixed point of the map \(x\mapsto qx+(1-q)c\). The hypothesis is required only for the first \(n\) indices, which is what allows the bound to be applied to the warmup phase of a schedule that changes after \(n\) steps. No condition \(q\le1\) is needed.

steps.title: The constant-step bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((r_k)_{k\ge0}\) be real numbers and \(a,t\in\mathbb R\) with \(a\ge0\), \(0\le t\le1\) and \(r_0\ge0\). Let \(n\in\mathbb N\) and suppose that

\[r_{j+1}\le\frac{1-t}{1+t}\,r_j+\frac{a\,t^2}{1+t}\qquad\text{for every }j<n.\qquad(3)\]

Then

\[r_n\le e^{-2tn}\,r_0+\frac{a\,t}2.\qquad(4)\]

In particular, if (3) holds for every \(j\in\mathbb N\), then (4) holds for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).

Proof. Put \(q=\frac{1-t}{1+t}\) and \(c=\frac{at}2\). Since \(0\le t\le1\), we have \(1+t>0\) and \(1-t\ge0\), hence \(q\ge0\); also \(c\ge0\) because \(a,t\ge0\). The forcing term in (3) equals \((1-q)c\):

\[(1-q)\,c=\frac{(1+t)-(1-t)}{1+t}\cdot\frac{at}2=\frac{2t}{1+t}\cdot\frac{at}2=\frac{a\,t^2}{1+t}.\]

Thus (3) is the hypothesis of Step 2 with these \(q\) and \(c\), and Step 2 gives \(r_n\le q^nr_0+\frac{at}2\). By Step 1, \(0\le q\le e^{-2t}\); raising to the power \(n\) preserves inequalities between nonnegative numbers, so \(q^n\le(e^{-2t})^n=e^{-2tn}\). Multiplying by \(r_0\ge0\) gives \(q^nr_0\le e^{-2tn}r_0\), which proves (4). The second assertion applies the first to each \(n\), the hypothesis for all \(j\) containing the hypothesis for \(j<n\). \(\square\)

With \(r_k=\frac mp\mathsf W_2^2(\nu_k,\pi)\), \(t=mh\) and \(a=\kappa_{\rm av}+1\), multiplying (4) by \(p/m\) gives \(\mathsf W_2^2(\nu_n,\pi)\le e^{-2mnh}\mathsf W_2^2(\nu_0,\pi)+\frac{(M_{\rm av}+m)hp}{2m}\), since \(\frac pm\cdot\frac{(\kappa_{\rm av}+1)mh}2=\frac{(M_{\rm av}+m)hp}{2m}\). This is the second claim of Theorem 1.

steps.title: The induction step of the decreasing-step schedule
steps.body:
Claim. (1) Let \(a,x,r\in\mathbb R\) with \(x\ge1\) and \(r\le a/x\). Then

\[\frac{1-1/x}{1+1/x}\,r+\frac{a\,(1/x)^2}{1+1/x}\le\frac a{x+1}.\]

(2) Let \((r_n)_{n\ge0}\) be real numbers and \(a,\kappa\in\mathbb R\) with \(a\ge0\), \(\kappa\ge1\) and \(r_0\le a/\kappa\). Suppose that for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), with \(t_n=1/(\kappa+n)\),

\[r_{n+1}\le\frac{1-t_n}{1+t_n}\,r_n+\frac{a\,t_n^2}{1+t_n}.\qquad(5)\]

Then \(r_n\le\frac a{\kappa+n}\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).

Proof. (1) Since \(x\ge1>0\), we have \(1/x\le1\) and \(1+1/x>0\), so the coefficient \(q=\frac{1-1/x}{1+1/x}\) is nonnegative. Multiplying \(r\le a/x\) by \(q\ge0\),

\[q\,r+\frac{a(1/x)^2}{1+1/x}\le q\,\frac ax+\frac{a(1/x)^2}{1+1/x}.\]

Multiplying numerators and denominators by \(x\) gives \(q=\frac{x-1}{x+1}\) and \(\frac{(1/x)^2}{1+1/x}=\frac1{x(x+1)}\), so the right-hand side equals

\[\frac{a(x-1)}{x(x+1)}+\frac a{x(x+1)}=\frac{a\,x}{x(x+1)}=\frac a{x+1}.\]

(2) Induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\) the claim is the hypothesis \(r_0\le a/\kappa\). Assume \(r_n\le a/(\kappa+n)\) and put \(x=\kappa+n\). Then \(x\ge1\) because \(\kappa\ge1\) and \(n\ge0\), and \(t_n=1/x\). By (5) and part (1),

\[r_{n+1}\le\frac{1-1/x}{1+1/x}\,r_n+\frac{a(1/x)^2}{1+1/x}\le\frac a{x+1}=\frac a{\kappa+(n+1)}.\qquad\square\]

Part (1) uses no sign condition on \(a\), and the hypothesis \(a\ge0\) of part (2) is not used in its proof. In Proposition 1, \(x=\kappa_\infty+k-k_0\) and \(t_n=mh_k\) is the decreasing step after the warmup phase; part (1) states that the bound \(a/x\) is propagated to \(a/(x+1)\) by one step of the schedule.

steps.title: The iteration count reaches the prescribed accuracy
steps.body:
Definition. For \(\kappa,a,\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon\in\mathbb R\), the iteration count of Proposition 1 is

\[k_\varepsilon=k_0(\kappa,a,\varepsilon_0)+\Bigl\lceil\max\Bigl(\frac a{\varepsilon^2}-\kappa,\,0\Bigr)\Bigr\rceil.\]

Claim. (1) Let \(\kappa>0\), \(a>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). If \(k\in\mathbb N\) satisfies \(k\ge k_\varepsilon\), then \(k\ge k_0\) and

\[\frac a{\kappa+(k-k_0)}\le\varepsilon^2.\]

(2) Under the hypotheses of Step 3 and \(\varepsilon>0\), \(r_k\le\varepsilon^2\) for every \(k\ge k_\varepsilon\).

\[k-k_0\ge N\ge\max\Bigl(\frac a{\varepsilon^2}-\kappa,0\Bigr)\ge\frac a{\varepsilon^2}-\kappa,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\kappa+(k-k_0)\ge\frac a{\varepsilon^2}.\]

The number \(\kappa+(k-k_0)\) is positive because \(\kappa>0\). Multiplying the last inequality by \(\varepsilon^2>0\) gives \(a\le\varepsilon^2(\kappa+(k-k_0))\), and dividing by \(\kappa+(k-k_0)>0\) gives the claim.

(2) Since \(\kappa\ge1>0\), part (1) gives \(k\ge k_0\) and \(a/(\kappa+(k-k_0))\le\varepsilon^2\). Step 3 gives \(r_k\le a/(\kappa+(k-k_0))\), and the two inequalities combine. \(\square\)

AverageLMC/SquaredTransport.lean.title: Couplings, the transport infimum and lifts of output couplings
AverageLMC/SquaredTransport.lean.summary:
This section contains two general facts about quadratic transport that are used when a one-step bound is proved by constructing couplings. Let \(E\) be a normed space with its Borel sets (in the applications \(E=\mathbb R^p\)). For measures \(\mu,\pi\) on \(E\), a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) is a measure \(\gamma\) on \(E\times E\) whose first and second marginals are \(\mu\) and \(\pi\). Its cost is \(C(\gamma)=\bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,\gamma(dx,dy)\bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,\infty]\), and the Wasserstein distance is \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)=\inf_\gamma C(\gamma)\in[0,\infty]\), the infimum over all couplings. No optimal coupling is assumed to exist.

The first result passes a bound from couplings to the distance: if \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\) and \(r\le a\,C(\gamma)^2+b\) for every coupling \(\gamma\) of finite cost, then \(r\le a\,\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)^2+b\), for every real coefficient \(a\). The second result lifts a coupling of an output law to the input space: if \(F:S\to E\) is measurable, \(P\) is a probability measure on \(S\) and \(\gamma\) couples the law \(P\circ F^{-1}\) of \(F\) with \(\pi\), then there is a probability measure \(R\) on \(S\times E\) with first marginal \(P\) under which the pair \((F(s),y)\) has law \(\gamma\). In the stochastic-gradient argument \(s\) is the input of one step, \(F(s)\) the full-gradient output, and the lift allows an independent random index to be adjoined to an arbitrary coupling of the full-gradient output with the target.

steps.title: From bounds over couplings to a bound on the squared distance
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu,\pi\) be measures on \(E\) with \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\), and write \(w=\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)\in[0,\infty)\). Let \(r,a,b\in\mathbb R\) and suppose that

\[r\le a\,C(\gamma)^2+b\qquad\text{for every coupling }\gamma\text{ of }\mu\text{ and }\pi\text{ with }C(\gamma)<\infty.\qquad(1)\]

Then \(r\le a\,w^2+b\). In particular, if \(\mu',\pi'\) are measures with \(\mathsf W_2(\mu',\pi')<\infty\) and \(\mathsf W_2(\mu',\pi')^2\le a\,C(\gamma)^2+b\) for every finite-cost coupling \(\gamma\) of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\), then \(\mathsf W_2(\mu',\pi')^2\le a\,\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)^2+b\).

Proof. Case \(a\ge0\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(w<w+\varepsilon\) and \(w\) is the infimum of the costs, some coupling \(\gamma\) satisfies \(C(\gamma)<w+\varepsilon\); in particular \(C(\gamma)<\infty\). Squaring the inequality between the nonnegative numbers \(C(\gamma)\) and \(w+\varepsilon\) gives \(C(\gamma)^2\le(w+\varepsilon)^2\), and multiplying by \(a\ge0\) and using (1),

\[r\le a\,C(\gamma)^2+b\le a\,(w+\varepsilon)^2+b.\]

This holds for every \(\varepsilon>0\). The function \(\varepsilon\mapsto a(w+\varepsilon)^2+b\) is continuous, so letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) gives \(r\le a\,w^2+b\).

Case \(a<0\). Since \(w<\infty\), not every coupling has infinite cost, for otherwise the infimum would be \(\infty\); hence there is a coupling \(\gamma\) with \(C(\gamma)<\infty\). By the definition of the infimum, \(w\le C(\gamma)\), hence \(w^2\le C(\gamma)^2\), and multiplying by \(a<0\) reverses this inequality: \(a\,C(\gamma)^2\le a\,w^2\). With (1), \(r\le a\,C(\gamma)^2+b\le a\,w^2+b\).

The second statement is the first with \(r=\mathsf W_2(\mu',\pi')^2\). \(\square\)

The finiteness assumption on \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)\) is needed in both cases: the approximation \(C(\gamma)<w+\varepsilon\) and the existence of a finite-cost coupling require a finite infimum. The case \(a<0\) occurs in Theorem 1 when \(1-mh<0\).

steps.title: Lifting an output coupling to the input space
steps.body:
Setting. Let \((S,\mathcal S)\) be a measurable space with a probability measure \(P\), let \(E\) be a standard Borel space (for instance \(\mathbb R^p\)), let \(F:S\to E\) be measurable, and let \(\gamma\) be a coupling of the law \(P\circ F^{-1}\) of \(F\) and a measure \(\pi\) on \(E\). Since the first marginal of \(\gamma\) is a probability measure, \(\gamma\) is a probability measure. Because \(E\) is standard Borel, \(\gamma\) admits a disintegration with respect to its first coordinate: a Markov kernel \(K\) from \(E\) to \(E\) (each \(K(x,\cdot)\) is a probability measure and \(x\mapsto K(x,B)\) is measurable) such that

\[\begin{aligned} \gamma(C)&=\int_E K(x,C_x)\,(P\circ F^{-1})(dx),\\ C_x&=\{y:(x,y)\in C\},\qquad C\subseteq E\times E\text{ measurable}. \qquad(2) \end{aligned}\]

Define the measure \(R\) on \(S\times E\) by

\[R(G)=\int_S K\bigl(F(s),G_s\bigr)\,P(ds),\qquad G_s=\{y:(s,y)\in G\},\]

that is, \(s\) is drawn from \(P\) and then \(y\) from \(K(F(s),\cdot)\).

Claim. (1) \(R\) is a probability measure. (2) The first marginal of \(R\) is \(P\). (3) The image of \(R\) under \((s,y)\mapsto(F(s),y)\) is \(\gamma\). (4) The second marginal of \(R\) is \(\pi\).

Proof. (1) and (2): for measurable \(A\subseteq S\), \(R(A\times E)=\int_AK(F(s),E)\,P(ds)=P(A)\), because \(K(F(s),E)=1\). Taking \(A=S\) gives \(R(S\times E)=1\).

(3) Let \(C\subseteq E\times E\) be measurable and \(G=\{(s,y):(F(s),y)\in C\}\). Then \(G_s=C_{F(s)}\), so

\[R(G)=\int_SK\bigl(F(s),C_{F(s)}\bigr)\,P(ds)=\int_EK(x,C_x)\,(P\circ F^{-1})(dx)=\gamma(C),\]

where the middle equality is the change-of-variables formula for the image measure \(P\circ F^{-1}\) applied to the measurable function \(x\mapsto K(x,C_x)\), and the last equality is (2).

(4) The second coordinate of \((F(s),y)\) is \(y\). Taking the image of the measure in (3) under the second projection, the second marginal of \(R\) equals the second marginal of \(\gamma\), which is \(\pi\). \(\square\)

In probabilistic terms: on the probability space \((S\times E,R)\), the coordinate \(s\) has law \(P\), the coordinate \(y\) has law \(\pi\), and \((F(s),y)\) has the prescribed joint law \(\gamma\). Every coupling of the output law with the target is therefore realized jointly with the input of the step.

AverageLMC/CenteredPerturbation.lean.title: Transport cost of a conditionally centred perturbation
AverageLMC/CenteredPerturbation.lean.summary:
This section proves the variance-addition inequality for quadratic transport that underlies the stochastic-gradient bound. Let \(s\) be a random input with law \(P\) on a measurable space \(S\), let \(i\) be an independent random index with law \(Q\) on a measurable space \(I\), let \(F(s)\) be an output in a Hilbert space \(E\) (for instance \(\mathbb R^p\)), and let \(D(s,i)\) be a perturbation whose mean over the index vanishes for every fixed input. Then, for every probability measure \(\pi\) on \(E\) with finite second moment,

\[\mathsf W_2^2\bigl(\mathcal L(F(s)+D(s,i)),\pi\bigr)\le\mathsf W_2^2\bigl(\mathcal L(F(s)),\pi\bigr)+\mathbb E\|D(s,i)\|^2,\]

where \(\mathcal L\) denotes the law under \(P\otimes Q\). For SGLD, \(s=(\vartheta,\xi)\), \(F(s)=\vartheta-h\nabla f(\vartheta)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi\) is the full-gradient Langevin output, \(i=I\) is the uniform data index and \(D=-h(g_I(\vartheta)-\nabla f(\vartheta))\) is the stochastic-gradient error. The proof uses an arbitrary finite-cost coupling of \(\mathcal L(F(s))\) with \(\pi\), lifts it to the input by the construction of the previous section, adjoins the independent index, and shows that the cross term of the squared distance vanishes.

steps.title: The squared \(L_2\) norm as an integral
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a measure space, \(E\) a real inner product space and \(f:\Omega\to E\) square integrable, \(\int\|f\|^2\,dP<\infty\) (with \(f\) almost everywhere strongly measurable). Let \(\|f\|_{L_2(P)}=\bigl(\int\|f\|^2\,dP\bigr)^{1/2}\), a finite nonnegative number. Then

\[\|f\|_{L_2(P)}^2=\int_\Omega\|f(\omega)\|^2\,P(d\omega).\]

Proof. Let \([f]\) denote the class of \(f\) in the Hilbert space \(L_2(P;E)\), whose inner product is \(\langle[g],[k]\rangle=\int\langle g(\omega),k(\omega)\rangle\,P(d\omega)\) and whose norm is \(\|f\|_{L_2(P)}\). Then

\[\|f\|_{L_2(P)}^2=\langle[f],[f]\rangle=\int_\Omega\langle f(\omega),f(\omega)\rangle\,P(d\omega)=\int_\Omega\|f(\omega)\|^2\,P(d\omega),\]

where the representative of \([f]\) used in the integral agrees with \(f\) almost everywhere, which does not change the integral. \(\square\)

The finiteness assumption matters because the \(L_2\) norm is defined with values in \([0,\infty]\): for a function that is not square integrable, the real number associated with \(\infty\) would be \(0\) and the identity would fail.

steps.title: Adding a centred perturbation adds its second moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(S\) and \(I\) be measurable spaces with probability measures \(P\) and \(Q\). Let \(E\) be a real Hilbert space that is standard Borel and second countable with its Borel sets (for instance \(\mathbb R^p\)). Let \(F:S\to E\) be measurable and square integrable for \(P\), and let \(D:S\times I\to E\) be jointly measurable and square integrable for \(P\otimes Q\), such that for every \(s\in S\) the function \(D(s,\cdot)\) is \(Q\)-integrable with

\[\int_ID(s,i)\,Q(di)=0.\qquad(1)\]

Let \(\pi\) be a probability measure on \(E\) with \(\int\|x\|^2\pi(dx)<\infty\), let \(\mu=P\circ F^{-1}\) be the law of \(F\), and let \(\nu\) be the law of \((s,i)\mapsto F(s)+D(s,i)\) under \(P\otimes Q\). Then \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)\) and \(\mathsf W_2(\nu,\pi)\) are finite and

\[\mathsf W_2(\nu,\pi)^2\le\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)^2+\int_{S\times I}\|D(s,i)\|^2\,(P\otimes Q)(ds,di).\]

Proof. Finiteness. The identity map has finite second moment under \(\mu\), because \(\int\|x\|^2\mu(dx)=\int\|F\|^2dP<\infty\), and under \(\nu\), because \(F(s)+D(s,i)\) is a sum of two square-integrable functions on \(S\times I\). For two probability measures with finite second moments the product coupling has finite cost, since \(\|x-y\|^2\le2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2\); hence \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\) and \(\mathsf W_2(\nu,\pi)<\infty\).

Reduction. By the first result of the previous section (with \(a=1\) and \(b=\int\|D\|^2d(P\otimes Q)\)), it suffices to show that \(\mathsf W_2(\nu,\pi)^2\le C(\gamma)^2+\int\|D\|^2d(P\otimes Q)\) for every coupling \(\gamma\) of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) with finite cost \(C(\gamma)\).

Construction. Fix such a \(\gamma\) and let \(R\) be the lifted coupling of the previous section: a probability measure on \(S\times E\) with first marginal \(P\), second marginal \(\pi\), under which \((F(s),y)\) has law \(\gamma\). Work on \((S\times E)\times I\) with the product probability \(R\otimes Q\) and the random variables

\[A=F(s)-y,\qquad B=D(s,i),\qquad X=F(s)+D(s,i),\qquad Y=y.\]

Since the first marginal of \(R\) is \(P\), the image of \(R\otimes Q\) under \(((s,y),i)\mapsto(s,i)\) is \(P\otimes Q\). Consequently \(X\) has law \(\nu\), and \(Y\) has law \(\pi\). Both \(A\) and \(B\) are square integrable: \(\int\|A\|^2d(R\otimes Q)=\int\|F(s)-y\|^2R(ds,dy)=\int\|x-y\|^2\gamma(dx,dy)=C(\gamma)^2<\infty\), where the first equality integrates out the probability measure \(Q\) and the second is the change of variables under \((s,y)\mapsto(F(s),y)\); and \(\int\|B\|^2d(R\otimes Q)=\int\|D\|^2d(P\otimes Q)\) by the change of variables under \(((s,y),i)\mapsto(s,i)\). We record these as

\[\int\|A\|^2\,d(R\otimes Q)=C(\gamma)^2,\qquad\int\|B\|^2\,d(R\otimes Q)=\int\|D\|^2\,d(P\otimes Q).\qquad(2)\]

The cross term vanishes. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(|\langle A,B\rangle|\le\|A\|\,\|B\|\), and \(\|A\|\,\|B\|\) is integrable as a product of two square-integrable functions (Hölder's inequality); so \(\langle A,B\rangle\) is integrable. By Fubini's theorem,

\[\int\langle A,B\rangle\,d(R\otimes Q)=\int_{S\times E}\Bigl(\int_I\bigl\langle F(s)-y,\,D(s,i)\bigr\rangle\,Q(di)\Bigr)R(ds,dy).\]

For fixed \((s,y)\), the map \(v\mapsto\langle F(s)-y,v\rangle\) is a continuous linear functional on \(E\), and continuous linear functionals commute with Bochner integrals of integrable functions. Using the integrability of \(D(s,\cdot)\) and (1), the inner integral equals \(\langle F(s)-y,\int_ID(s,i)Q(di)\rangle=\langle F(s)-y,0\rangle=0\). Hence \(\int\langle A,B\rangle\,d(R\otimes Q)=0\).

Energy identity. Pointwise \(\|A+B\|^2=\|A\|^2+2\langle A,B\rangle+\|B\|^2\), and the three terms are integrable. Integrating and using the vanishing of the cross term and (2),

\[\int\|A+B\|^2\,d(R\otimes Q)=C(\gamma)^2+\int\|D\|^2\,d(P\otimes Q).\qquad(3)\]

Conclusion. The pair \((X,Y)\) defines a coupling of \(\nu\) and \(\pi\), and \(X-Y=A+B\). Therefore \(\mathsf W_2(\nu,\pi)\le\bigl(\int\|A+B\|^2d(R\otimes Q)\bigr)^{1/2}\). Squaring this inequality between nonnegative numbers, using the identity of Step 1 for the square-integrable function \(A+B\), and inserting (3) gives the required bound. \(\square\)

Two hypotheses deserve comment. Condition (1) must hold for every input \(s\), not only on average; it is what makes the cross term vanish after integrating out the index. The finiteness of the second moment of \(\pi\) is used only to make both distances finite, so that the bound over couplings passes to the distance.

AverageLMC/ExtendedTransport.lean.title: Affine transport bounds for arbitrary initial distributions
AverageLMC/ExtendedTransport.lean.summary: The main theorems are stated for every initial probability distribution, including distributions at infinite Wasserstein distance from the target. For this purpose distances are taken in the extended half-line \([0,\infty]\), with the conventions \(x+\infty=\infty\) and \(c\cdot\infty=\infty\) for \(c>0\). This section shows that an affine bound \(\mathsf W_2^2(\mu',\pi')\le a\,\mathsf W_2^2(\mu,\pi)+b\), proved under the assumption \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\), holds in \([0,\infty]\) without that assumption, provided \(a>0\) and \(b\ge0\): if the initial distance is infinite, the right-hand side is infinite. No moment assumption on the initial distribution is therefore needed in the final statements.

steps.title: Extending a finite-distance bound to infinite initial distance
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu,\pi,\mu',\pi'\) be measures on a normed space \(E\), and let \(a>0\) and \(b\ge0\). Assume that, whenever \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\), also \(\mathsf W_2(\mu',\pi')<\infty\) and

\[\mathsf W_2(\mu',\pi')^2\le a\,\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)^2+b\qquad\text{(an inequality between real numbers).}\]

Then, in \([0,\infty]\), \(\mathsf W_2(\mu',\pi')^2\le a\,\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)^2+b\) holds without any finiteness assumption.

Proof. If \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)=\infty\), then \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)^2=\infty\) and \(a\cdot\infty=\infty\) because \(a>0\), so the right-hand side is \(\infty\) and the inequality holds. If \(\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\), then by assumption \(\mathsf W_2(\mu',\pi')<\infty\), so both distances are real numbers and the real inequality holds. The inclusion of \([0,\infty)\) into \([0,\infty]\) preserves order, sums and products of nonnegative numbers; since \(a\,\mathsf W_2(\mu,\pi)^2\ge0\) and \(b\ge0\), the real inequality is also an inequality in \([0,\infty]\). \(\square\)

Both sign conditions are needed. If \(a=0\), then \(0\cdot\infty=0\) in \([0,\infty]\) and an infinite initial distance would not make the right-hand side infinite. If \(b<0\), the right-hand side could not be interpreted in \([0,\infty]\).

AverageLMC/SGLDLaw.lean.title: The SGLD transition and its variance decomposition
AverageLMC/SGLDLaw.lean.summary:
This section defines the stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics with fixed-point control variates and proves the variance decomposition on which its analysis rests. The potential is a finite sum \(f=\sum_{i=1}^nf_i\) of functions \(f_i:\mathbb R^p o\mathbb R\), and \( heta_*\in\mathbb R^p\) is a point with \( abla f( heta_*)=0\) (the minimizer of \(f\) in the application). The control-variate estimator of \( abla f(x)\) and its error are

\[g_i(x)=n igl( abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*) igr),\qquad e_i(x)=g_i(x)- abla f(x)\qquad(i=1,\dots,n).\]

One SGLD step from \(\vartheta\sim u\) is \(\vartheta^+=\vartheta-h\,g_I(\vartheta)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi\), where \(\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) and the index \(I\), uniform on \(\{1,\dots,n\}\), are independent of each other and of \(\vartheta\); \( u^+\) denotes the law of \(\vartheta^+\), and \( u_k\) the law after \(k\) steps with fresh innovations. Writing \( u^+_{ m LMC}\) for the law of the full-gradient step \(\vartheta-h abla f(\vartheta)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi\), the main result is

\[\mathsf W_2^2( u^+,\pi)\le\mathsf W_2^2( u^+_{ m LMC},\pi)+h^2\,\mathbb E\|e_I(\vartheta)\|^2,\qquad\mathbb E\|e_I(\vartheta)\|^2=\mathbb E\|g_I(\vartheta)\|^2-\mathbb E\| abla f(\vartheta)\|^2,\]

for every probability measure \(\pi\) with finite second moment, together with \(\mathbb E\|g_I(\vartheta)\|^2=n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E\| abla f_i(\vartheta)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|^2\). The SGLD step is thus the LMC step plus a perturbation that is centred given \((\vartheta,\xi)\), and the variance-addition inequality of the previous sections applies. The section also checks that all laws involved are probability measures with finite second moments.

steps.title: The update, the transition and the chain of laws
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(n,p\in\mathbb N\), \(f_1,\dots,f_n:\mathbb R^p o\mathbb R\), \(f=\sum_if_i\), \( heta_*\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\) (with \(\sqrt{2h}\) read as \(0\) if \(h<0\); only \(h\ge0\) is of interest). The SGLD update map is

\[\Phi(x,z,i)=x-h\,g_i(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\qquad(x,z\in\mathbb R^p,\ i\in\{1,\dots,n\}).\]

For a measure \( u\) on \(\mathbb R^p\), the SGLD transition gives the image measure \( u^+=( u\otimes\gamma_p\otimes U_n)\circ\Phi^{-1}\), where \(\gamma_p=\mathcal N(0,I_p)\) is the standard Gaussian measure and \(U_n\) the uniform probability on \(\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(U_n(\{i\})=1/n\). The chain of laws is \( u_0= u\), \( u_{k+1}=( u_k)^+\); each step uses a new independent pair \((\xi,I)\).

Claim. (1) For all \(x,z,i\),

\[\Phi(x,z,i)= igl(x-h abla f(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z igr)+(-h)\,e_i(x).\qquad(1)\]

(2) If every \(f_i\) is differentiable with Lipschitz gradient and \( abla f\) is Lipschitz, then \(\Phi\) is measurable on \(\mathbb R^p imes\mathbb R^p imes\{1,\dots,n\}\).

(3) If \(n\ge1\) and \( u\) is a probability measure, then \( u^+\) and every \( u_k\) are probability measures.

Proof. (1) By definition \(g_i(x)=e_i(x)+ abla f(x)\), so \(-h\,g_i(x)=-h abla f(x)+(-h)e_i(x)\); insert this in \(\Phi\).

(2) By (1), \(\Phi\) is the sum of \((x,z)\mapsto x-h abla f(x)+\sqrt{2h}z\), which is continuous because \( abla f\) is Lipschitz, and \((x,i)\mapsto-h\,e_i(x)\). For each fixed \(i\) the map \(x\mapsto e_i(x)=n( abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*))- abla f(x)\) is continuous, and a function on \(\mathbb R^p imes\{1,\dots,n\}\) whose sections are measurable is measurable, since \(\{1,\dots,n\}\) is finite with all subsets measurable. Sums of measurable functions are measurable.

(3) For \(n\ge1\), \(U_n\) is a probability measure (it gives mass \(1/n\) to each of the \(n\) points). The product \( u\otimes\gamma_p\otimes U_n\) of probability measures is a probability measure, and so is its image under \(\Phi\). Induction on \(k\) gives the statement for \( u_k\): \( u_0= u\), and if \( u_k\) is a probability measure, so is \( u_{k+1}=( u_k)^+\). \(\square\)

Identity (1) displays the SGLD step as the LMC step of Theorem 1 plus the perturbation \(-h\,e_I(\vartheta)\); everything that follows is built on it.

steps.title: Second moments are preserved
steps.body:
Claim. Let \( u\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb R^p\) with finite second moment, \(\int\|x\|^2 u(dx)<\infty\).

  1. If \(F:\mathbb R^p o\mathbb R\) has an \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(M\ge0\), then \( abla F\) is square integrable for \( u\).
  2. Under the same hypothesis on \(F\) and for every \(h\in\mathbb R\), the map \((x,z)\mapsto x-h abla F(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\) is square integrable for \( u\otimes\gamma_p\).
  3. If every \(f_i\) is differentiable with Lipschitz gradient and \( abla f\) is Lipschitz, then \( u^+\) has finite second moment.

Proof. (1) The Lipschitz bound and the triangle inequality give \(\| abla F(x)\|\le\| abla F(0)\|+M\|x\|\), hence \(\| abla F(x)\|^2\le2\| abla F(0)\|^2+2M^2\|x\|^2\) by \((u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2\). The right-hand side is \( u\)-integrable because \( u\) is a probability measure with finite second moment. (Measurability holds because \( abla F\) is continuous.)

(2) Under \( u\otimes\gamma_p\), the coordinate \(x\) is square integrable by assumption, \( abla F(x)\) is square integrable by (1), and \(z\) is square integrable because \(\int\|z\|^2\gamma_p(dz)=p<\infty\). Square-integrable functions form a vector space, so the linear combination \(x-h abla F(x)+\sqrt{2h}z\) is square integrable.

(3) By the change-of-variables formula, \(\int\|y\|^2 u^+(dy)=\int\|\Phi\|^2\,d( u\otimes\gamma_p\otimes U_n)\), so it suffices that \(\Phi\) is square integrable. By (1) of Step 1, \(\Phi\) is the full-gradient map, square integrable by (2) applied to \(F=f\), plus \(-h\,e_i(x)\). For each \(i\), \(e_i(x)=n( abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*))-\sum_k abla f_k(x)\) is square integrable in \(x\) by (1) applied to the \(f_k\) (constants are square integrable for a probability measure), and since there are finitely many indices, \(\|e_i(x)\|^2\le\sum_{k=1}^n\|e_k(x)\|^2\) shows that \((x,z,i)\mapsto e_i(x)\) is square integrable for \( u\otimes\gamma_p\otimes U_n\). \(\square\)

These facts are what make the transport distances in the next step finite; no moment assumption beyond that of \( u\) is needed.

steps.title: Variance addition for one SGLD step
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(n\ge1\), let every \(f_i\) be differentiable with Lipschitz gradient, let \( abla f\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz, and let \( abla f( heta_*)=0\). Let \(h\in\mathbb R\), and let \( u\) and \(\pi\) be probability measures on \(\mathbb R^p\) with finite second moments. Let \( u^+_{ m LMC}\) be the law of \(x-h abla f(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\) under \( u\otimes\gamma_p\). Then

\[\mathsf W_2( u^+,\pi)^2\le\mathsf W_2( u^+_{ m LMC},\pi)^2+h^2\int\|e_i(x)\|^2\,( u\otimes\gamma_p\otimes U_n)(dx,dz,di),\qquad(2)\]

and

\[\int\|e_i(x)\|^2\,d( u\otimes\gamma_p\otimes U_n)=\int\|g_i(x)\|^2\,( u\otimes U_n)(dx,di)-\int\| abla f(x)\|^2\, u(dx).\qquad(3)\]

Proof. Pointwise facts for fixed \(x\). Since each \(f_i\) is differentiable, \( abla f=\sum_i abla f_i\). Averaging over the index and using \( abla f( heta_*)=0\),

\[ rac1n\sum_{i=1}^ng_i(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n igl( abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*) igr)= abla f(x)- abla f( heta_*)= abla f(x),\]

so the estimator is unbiased and \( rac1n\sum_ie_i(x)=0\). Expanding \(\|g_i(x)- abla f(x)\|^2\) and averaging,

\[ egin{aligned} rac1n\sum_i\|e_i(x)\|^2 &= rac1n\sum_i\|g_i(x)\|^2\ &\quad-2\Bigl\langle rac1n\sum_ig_i(x), abla f(x)\Bigr angle +\| abla f(x)\|^2\ &= rac1n\sum_i\|g_i(x)\|^2-\| abla f(x)\|^2. \qquad(4) \end{aligned}\]

Proof of (2). Apply the centred-perturbation inequality of the earlier section with \(S=\mathbb R^p imes\mathbb R^p\), \(P= u\otimes\gamma_p\), index space \(\{1,\dots,n\}\) with \(Q=U_n\), \(F(x,z)=x-h abla f(x)+\sqrt{2h}z\) and \(D((x,z),i)=-h\,e_i(x)\). Its hypotheses hold: \(F\) is continuous, hence measurable, and square integrable by Step 2; \(D\) is jointly measurable and square integrable by Steps 1 and 2; for fixed \((x,z)\), \(D((x,z),\cdot)\) is integrable (the index set is finite) and its mean \(-h\cdot rac1n\sum_ie_i(x)\) is \(0\); and \(\pi\) is a probability measure with finite second moment. By (1) of Step 1, the law of \(F+D\) under \(P\otimes Q\) is \( u^+\), and the law of \(F\) under \(P\) is \( u^+_{ m LMC}\). Finally \(\|D\|^2=h^2\|e_i(x)\|^2\), and the constant \(h^2\) comes out of the integral. This gives (2).

Proof of (3). The integrand \(\|e_i(x)\|^2\) is integrable by Step 2. By Fubini's theorem we may integrate first over the index; by (4) this gives the function \(x\mapsto\int\|g_i(x)\|^2U_n(di)-\| abla f(x)\|^2\), which does not depend on \(z\). Integrating it against the probability measure \(\gamma_p\) leaves it unchanged, and integrating over \( u\), splitting the difference (both terms are integrable by Step 2) and using Fubini's theorem once more for \(\int\!\int\|g_i(x)\|^2U_n(di)\, u(dx)\) gives (3). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \( abla f( heta_*)=0\) is used only for the unbiasedness of the estimator, and hence for the vanishing of the cross term. The inequality is between real numbers; Step 2 guarantees that all distances are finite.

steps.title: The second moment of the estimator
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(n\ge1\), let every \( abla f_i\) be Lipschitz, let \( heta_*\in\mathbb R^p\), and let \( u\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb R^p\) with finite second moment. Then

\[\int\|g_i(x)\|^2\,( u\otimes U_n)(dx,di)=n\sum_{i=1}^n\int\| abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|^2\, u(dx).\]

\[\int\|g_i(x)\|^2\,U_n(di)= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n n^2\| abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|^2=n\sum_{i=1}^n\| abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|^2.\]

The function \((x,i)\mapsto\|g_i(x)\|^2\) is integrable for \( u\otimes U_n\) (Step 2), so by Fubini's theorem its integral equals the \( u\)-integral of the last display. Each \(x\mapsto\| abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|^2\) is \( u\)-integrable by (1) of Step 2, so the integral of the finite sum is the sum of the integrals, and the constant \(n\) comes out of the integral. \(\square\)

With (3) of Step 3, \(h^2\mathbb E\|e_I(\vartheta)\|^2=nh^2\sum_i\| abla f_i(\vartheta)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|_{L_2}^2-h^2\| abla f(\vartheta)\|_{L_2}^2\); this is the last term of the first claim of Proposition 3 of the paper, together with the extra \(-h^2\| abla f(\vartheta)\|_{L_2}^2\) that changes the coefficient \(h^2(hM_\infty-1)\) of Theorem 1 into \(h^2(hM_\infty-2)\).

AverageLMC/SGLDRecurrence.lean.title: The scalar SGLD recurrence
AverageLMC/SGLDRecurrence.lean.summary:
This section carries out the scalar part of the constant-step SGLD theorem. The letters denote real numbers: \(m>0\) is the strong convexity constant of the full potential \(f=\sum_if_i\), \(R=nM_{\rm rms}\), \(A\ge0\) is the average coordinate smoothness of \(f\), \(h\ge0\) the step and \(p\ge0\) the dimension. Under the step condition \(3R^2h\le m\) of the paper (equivalent to \(h\le\bar m/(3nM_{\rm rms}^2)\) with \(m=n\bar m\)) and \(m^2\le R^2\), we prove

\[\frac{1-mh}{1+mh}+2R^2h^2\le\frac1{1+mh},\qquad\Bigl(\frac{A+m}{1+mh}+\frac{2R^2}m\Bigr)h^2p\le\frac{(A+2m+2R^2/m)\,h^2p}{1+mh},\]

and deduce that every nonnegative sequence satisfying the one-step SGLD recurrence obeys

\[r_k\le(1+mh)^{-k}r_0+\frac{(A+2m+2R^2/m)\,hp}{m}.\]

With \(m=n\bar m\), \(R=nM_{\rm rms}\) and \(A=n\bar M_{\rm av}\), the last term is \((\bar M_{\rm av}+2\bar m+2M_{\rm rms}^2/\bar m)\,hp/\bar m\), the persistent error of the SGLD theorem. The recurrence itself is proved for the SGLD laws in a later section.

steps.title: Comparison of the contraction and forcing coefficients
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\), \(h\ge0\) and \(R\in\mathbb R\) with \(3R^2h\le m\).

  1. If \(m^2\le R^2\), then \(mh\le\frac13\).
  2. If \(m^2\le R^2\), then \(\displaystyle\frac{1-mh}{1+mh}+2R^2h^2\le\frac1{1+mh}\).
  3. For all \(A\in\mathbb R\) and \(p\ge0\), \[\Bigl(\frac{A+m}{1+mh}+\frac{2R^2}m\Bigr)h^2p\le\frac{(A+2m+2R^2/m)\,h^2p}{1+mh}.\]

Proof. Write \(t=mh\ge0\); then \(1+t>0\).

(1) Multiplying \(m^2\le R^2\) by \(h\ge0\) gives \(m^2h\le R^2h\), so \(3m^2h\le3R^2h\le m\), that is, \(m(3mh-1)\le0\). Since \(m>0\), this forces \(3mh-1\le0\).

(2) Multiplying by \(1+t>0\), the claim is equivalent to \((1-t)+2R^2h^2(1+t)\le1\), that is, to \(2R^2h^2(1+t)\le t\). Multiplying \(3R^2h\le m\) by \(h\ge0\) gives \(3R^2h^2\le t\). By (1), \(1+t\le\frac43\), and \(2R^2h^2\ge0\), so

\[2R^2h^2(1+t)\le\frac43\cdot2R^2h^2=\frac89\cdot3R^2h^2\le\frac89\,t\le t,\]

where the last inequality uses \(t\ge0\).

(3) It suffices to prove the inequality between the coefficients of \(h^2p\) and then multiply by \(h^2p\ge0\). Multiplying by \(1+t>0\), the coefficient inequality is equivalent to

\[(A+m)+\frac{2R^2}m(1+t)\le A+2m+\frac{2R^2}m,\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad\frac{2R^2}m\,t\le m.\]

Since \(\frac{2R^2}m\,t=2R^2h\), and \(2R^2h\le3R^2h\le m\) because \(R^2h\ge0\), the inequality holds. \(\square\)

Part (2) shows that the SGLD contraction factor, which is the LMC factor \(\frac{1-mh}{1+mh}\) increased by the stochastic-gradient contribution \(2R^2h^2\), is still at most \((1+mh)^{-1}<1\). Part (1) is used for this purpose; in the application \(m^2\le R^2\) is \(\bar m\le M_{\rm rms}\).

steps.title: Iteration of the SGLD recurrence
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\), \(h\ge0\), \(p\ge0\), \(A\ge0\) and \(R\in\mathbb R\) with \(m^2\le R^2\) and \(3R^2h\le m\). Let \((r_k)_{k\ge0}\) be nonnegative real numbers such that, for every \(k\),

\[r_{k+1}\le\Bigl(\frac{1-mh}{1+mh}+2R^2h^2\Bigr)r_k+\Bigl(\frac{A+m}{1+mh}+\frac{2R^2}m\Bigr)h^2p.\qquad(1)\]

Then for every \(k\in\mathbb N\),

\[r_k\le(1+mh)^{-k}r_0+\frac{(A+2m+2R^2/m)\,hp}m.\]

Proof. Put \(q=(1+mh)^{-1}\) and \(c=(A+2m+2R^2/m)hp/m\). Then \(q\ge0\), and \(c\ge0\) because \(A,m,h,p\ge0\) and \(R^2/m\ge0\). We verify the hypothesis of the finite-horizon affine iteration of the scalar-recurrence section, \(r_{j+1}\le q\,r_j+(1-q)c\) for every \(j\). Multiplying part (2) of Step 1 by \(r_j\ge0\) bounds the first term of (1) by \(q\,r_j\). Part (3) of Step 1 bounds the second term by \((A+2m+2R^2/m)h^2p/(1+mh)\), and this equals \((1-q)c\):

\[(1-q)\,c=\frac{mh}{1+mh}\cdot\frac{(A+2m+2R^2/m)\,hp}m=\frac{(A+2m+2R^2/m)\,h^2p}{1+mh}.\]

Hence \(r_{j+1}\le q\,r_j+(1-q)c\) for every \(j\), and the affine iteration gives \(r_k\le q^kr_0+c\), which is the claim since \(q^k=(1+mh)^{-k}\). \(\square\)

The nonnegativity of the \(r_k\) is used to multiply the contraction inequality; in the application \(r_k=\mathsf W_2^2(\nu_k,\pi)\).

steps.body:
Claim. Let \(p,n\ge1\), let each \(f_i\) be differentiable with Lipschitz gradient, let \(f=\sum_if_i\) be \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\) and have an \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient (\(M\ge0\)), let \(h\ge0\), and let \( heta_*\) satisfy \( abla f( heta_*)=0\). Let \(\pi\) be the Gibbs measure of \(f\) and \( u\) a probability measure with \(\mathsf W_2( u,\pi)<\infty\). Then, with \(G=\int\| abla f\|^2d u\) and \(M_{ m av}\) the average coordinate smoothness of \(f\),

\[\mathsf W_2^2( u^+,\pi)\le rac{1-mh}{1+mh}\,\mathsf W_2^2( u,\pi)+ rac{(M_{ m av}+m)h^2p}{1+mh}+ rac{h^2(hM-2)}{1+mh}\,G+h^2\int\|g_i(x)\|^2\,( u\otimes U_n)(dx,di).\]

Proof. Preliminaries. \(f\) is differentiable as a finite sum of differentiable functions. The Gibbs measure of a differentiable strongly convex potential is a probability measure with finite second moment. Because \(\mathsf W_2( u,\pi)<\infty\), there is a coupling \(\gamma\) of \( u\) and \(\pi\) with \(\int\|x-y\|^2d\gamma<\infty\); from \(\|x\|^2\le2\|x-y\|^2+2\|y\|^2\) it follows that \( u\) has a finite second moment.

Two inequalities. The variance decomposition of SGLD (inequalities (2) and (3) of its section) gives

\[\mathsf W_2^2( u^+,\pi)\le\mathsf W_2^2( u^+_{ m LMC},\pi)+h^2\int\|g_i\|^2\,d( u\otimes U_n)-h^2G.\qquad(1)\]

The one-step bound of Theorem 1 for the full-gradient step gives

\[\mathsf W_2^2( u^+_{ m LMC},\pi)\le rac{1-mh}{1+mh}\,\mathsf W_2^2( u,\pi)+ rac{(M_{ m av}+m)h^2p}{1+mh}+ rac{h^2(hM-1)}{1+mh}\,G.\qquad(2)\]

The coefficient of \(G\). Inserting (2) into (1), \(G\) appears with the coefficient \( rac{h^2(hM-1)}{1+mh}-h^2\). Multiplying by \(1+mh>0\),

\[h^2(hM-1)-h^2(1+mh)=h^2(hM-2)-mh^3\le h^2(hM-2),\]

because \(mh^3\ge0\). Hence \( rac{h^2(hM-1)}{1+mh}-h^2\le rac{h^2(hM-2)}{1+mh}\), and multiplying by \(G\ge0\) and combining (1) and (2) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The last term is \(nh^2\sum_i\| abla f_i(\vartheta)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|_{L_2}^2\) by the estimator identity of the SGLD transition section, so this is the first claim of Proposition 3. No bound on the estimator variance is used yet.

Claim. (1) In addition to the hypotheses of Step 1, assume \(hM\le2\) and that \( heta_*\) is a global minimizer of \(f\), \(f( heta_*)\le f(x)\) for all \(x\). Then, with \(R=nM_{ m rms}\),

If \( u\) is a probability measure with \(\mathsf W_2( u,\pi)<\infty\), then \(\mathsf W_2( u_k,\pi)<\infty\) for every \(k\).

The estimator moment. For each \(x\), by the definition of the gradient seminorm, \(\| abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|\le M_\infty(f_i)\|x- heta_*\|\), so

\[\int\|g_i(x)\|^2U_n(di)=n\sum_{i=1}^n\| abla f_i(x)- abla f_i( heta_*)\|^2\le n\sum_{i=1}^nM_\infty(f_i)^2\,\|x- heta_*\|^2=R^2\|x- heta_*\|^2,\]

\[\int\|g_i(x)\|^2\,d( u\otimes U_n)\le R^2\int\|x- heta_*\|^2\, u(dx).\]

The moment around the minimizer. For a global minimizer \( heta_*\) of the strongly convex \(f\), the section on the initial moment proves \(\int\|x- heta_*\|^2 u(dx)\le2\mathsf W_2^2( u,\pi)+2p/m\). Hence

\[h^2\int\|g_i\|^2\,d( u\otimes U_n)\le h^2R^2\Bigl(2\mathsf W_2^2( u,\pi)+ rac{2p}m\Bigr)=2R^2h^2\,\mathsf W_2^2( u,\pi)+ rac{2R^2}m\,h^2p.\]

Adding this to the remaining terms of Step 1 and grouping \( rac{(M_{ m av}+m)h^2p}{1+mh}+ rac{2R^2}mh^2p\) gives the claim.

(2) Induction on \(k\). For \(k=0\) this is the hypothesis. steps.title: The constant-step bound
steps.body:
Claim. (1) Let \(p,n\ge1\), let each \(f_i\) be differentiable with Lipschitz gradient, let \(m>0\), \(h\ge0\), let \(f\) be \(m\)-strongly convex, let \(R=nM_{\rm rms}\) satisfy \(3R^2h\le m\), let \(\theta_*\) be a global minimizer of \(f\), and let \(\nu\) be a probability measure with \(\mathsf W_2(\nu,\pi)<\infty\). Then for every \(k\in\mathbb N\),

\[\mathsf W_2^2(\nu_k,\pi)\le(1+mh)^{-k}\,\mathsf W_2^2(\nu,\pi)+\Bigl(M_{\rm av}+2m+\frac{2R^2}m\Bigr)\frac{hp}m.\]

(2) Let \(\bar m>0\), let \(f\) be \(n\bar m\)-strongly convex and let \(0\le h\le\bar m/(3nM_{\rm rms}^2)\); keep the other hypotheses of (1). Then for every \(k\),

\[\mathsf W_2^2(\nu_k,\pi)\le(1+n\bar mh)^{-k}\,\mathsf W_2^2(\nu,\pi)+\Bigl(\frac{M_{\rm av}}n+2\bar m+\frac{2M_{\rm rms}^2}{\bar m}\Bigr)\frac{hp}{\bar m}.\]

Proof. (1) We collect the facts needed for Step 2 and for the scalar SGLD recurrence.

  • \(\nabla f\) is \(R\)-Lipschitz: \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le\sum_iM_\infty(f_i)\|x-y\|\le\sqrt{n\sum_iM_\infty(f_i)^2}\,\|x-y\|=R\|x-y\|\), by the triangle inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in \(\mathbb R^n\) (proved in the estimator section).
  • \(m\le R\) (also proved there, from \(m\le M_\infty(f)\le R\)); hence \(R>0\) and \(m^2\le R^2\).
  • \(hR\le\frac13\): indeed \(R(3Rh-1)=3R^2h-R\le m-R\le0\), and \(R>0\) forces \(3Rh\le1\). In particular the step condition \(hR\le2\) of Step 2 holds with \(M=R\).
  • \(\nabla f(\theta_*)=0\): a global minimizer is a local minimizer, and the derivative of a differentiable function vanishes at a local minimizer.
  • \(M_{\rm av}\ge m>0\), by the comparison of constants in the first section.

Let \(r_j=\mathsf W_2^2(\nu_j,\pi)\), finite by Step 2 (2). Applying Step 2 (1) to \(\nu_j\) (with \(M=R\)) gives, for every \(j\),

\[r_{j+1}\le\Bigl(\frac{1-mh}{1+mh}+2R^2h^2\Bigr)r_j+\Bigl(\frac{M_{\rm av}+m}{1+mh}+\frac{2R^2}m\Bigr)h^2p.\]

The \(r_j\) are nonnegative, \(A=M_{\rm av}\ge0\), \(p\ge0\), \(m^2\le R^2\) and \(3R^2h\le m\), so the iteration of the scalar SGLD recurrence applies and gives the claim.

(2) Put \(m=n\bar m>0\). Since \(n\bar m\le nM_{\rm rms}\) by (1), \(M_{\rm rms}\ge\bar m>0\), so \(3nM_{\rm rms}^2>0\) and the step condition is equivalent to \(3nM_{\rm rms}^2h\le\bar m\); multiplying by \(n\) gives \(3R^2h\le m\). Part (1) applies, and

\[\Bigl(M_{\rm av}+2n\bar m+\frac{2n^2M_{\rm rms}^2}{n\bar m}\Bigr)\frac{hp}{n\bar m}=\Bigl(\frac{M_{\rm av}}n+2\bar m+\frac{2M_{\rm rms}^2}{\bar m}\Bigr)\frac{hp}{\bar m}.\qquad\square\]

AverageLMC/LaplacianWeakChain.lean.title: Weighted weak consistency of the Euler chain
AverageLMC/LaplacianWeakChain.lean.summary:
This section proves a weak consistency estimate for the Euler (unadjusted Langevin) chain that is the discrete input of the Dynkin identity used in the proof of Theorem 2. Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space (in the application \(H=\mathbb R^p\)), \(\gamma\) the standard Gaussian measure on \(H\), \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) a potential with Lipschitz gradient and

\[X_{k+1}=X_k-h\nabla U(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,W_k\qquad(k\ge0),\]

where \(W_0,W_1,\dots\) are independent with law \(\gamma\) and independent of \((w,X_0)\) for a bounded random weight \(w\). For a test function \(\varphi\in C^2\) with \(\varphi\) and \(\mathcal L\varphi=\Delta\varphi-\langle\nabla U,\nabla\varphi\rangle\) bounded, write \(T(F,X)=\mathbb E[w\,F(X)]\). Assuming a uniform Gaussian Taylor estimate for \(\varphi\) with constants \(\varepsilon,K\) (proved elsewhere for compactly supported \(\varphi\)), we show

\[\Bigl|T(\varphi,X_n)-T(\varphi,X_0)-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}h\,T(\mathcal L\varphi,X_k)\Bigr|\le A\,(nh)\,(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h)\,(1+R^2)\]

whenever \(|w|\le A\) almost surely, \(0\le h\le1\), and \(\|\nabla U(X_k)\|_{L_2}\le R\) for \(k\le n\). The weight \(w\) carries arbitrary bounded information about the initial state; it is needed because the Dynkin identity is applied to test functions multiplied by a function of the initial coupling. The proof combines the independence of each new Gaussian increment from the past (including the weight), Fubini's theorem, and a telescoping sum.

steps.title: One Euler step with a fresh Gaussian increment and a bounded weight
steps.body:
Throughout, \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) is a probability space and \(\gamma\) is the standard Gaussian measure on \(H\).

Claim. (1) Let \(w,F:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) be measurable, \(A\ge0\), \(C\in\mathbb R\), with \(|w|\le A\) almost surely and \(|F|\le C\) everywhere. Then \(wF\) is \(P\)-integrable.

(2) Let \(\varphi:H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous with \(|\varphi|\le C\), \(b:H\to H\) measurable, \(x,z:\Omega\to H\) and \(w:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) measurable with \(|w|\le A\) almost surely (\(A\ge0\)), and assume that the joint law of \(((w,x),z)\) is the product of the law of \((w,x)\) and \(\gamma\) (that is, \(z\sim\gamma\) is independent of \((w,x)\)). Then for every \(h\in\mathbb R\) (with \(\sqrt{2h}=0\) for \(h<0\)),

\[\mathbb E\bigl[w\,\varphi\bigl(x+hb(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\bigr)\bigr]=\mathbb E\Bigl[w\int_H\varphi\bigl(x+hb(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,y\bigr)\,\gamma(dy)\Bigr].\]

(3) In the setting of (2), let in addition \(\varphi\in C^2\), \(b(x)\in L_2(P)\), and \(w\,(D\varphi(x)b(x)+\Delta\varphi(x))\) integrable. Let \(\varepsilon>0\), \(K\ge0\), and assume the uniform Gaussian Taylor estimate

\[\Bigl|\int\varphi(y+hv+\sqrt{2h}\,u)\,\gamma(du)-\varphi(y)-h\bigl(D\varphi(y)v+\Delta\varphi(y)\bigr)\Bigr|\le h(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h)(1+\|v\|^2)\qquad(1)\]

for all \(y,v\in H\) and \(0\le h\le1\). Then for \(0\le h\le1\),

\[\begin{gathered} \left|\begin{aligned} &\mathbb E\bigl[w\varphi(x+hb(x)+\sqrt{2h}z)\bigr]-\mathbb E[w\varphi(x)]\\ &\quad-h\,\mathbb E\bigl[w\bigl(D\varphi(x)b(x)+\Delta\varphi(x)\bigr)\bigr] \end{aligned}\right|\\ \le A\,h\,(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h)\bigl(1+\mathbb E\|b(x)\|^2\bigr). \end{gathered}\]

Proof. (1) \(wF\) is measurable and \(|wF|\le AC\) almost surely; a constant is integrable for a probability measure, so \(wF\) is integrable by domination.

(2) Let \(G((s,u),y)=s\,\varphi(u+hb(u)+\sqrt{2h}y)\) on \((\mathbb R\times H)\times H\), a measurable function. By the change-of-variables formula and the product form of the law,

\[\mathbb E\bigl[G((w,x),z)\bigr]=\int G\,d\bigl(\mathcal L(w,x)\otimes\gamma\bigr)=\int_{\Omega\times H}w(a)\,\varphi\bigl(x(a)+hb(x(a))+\sqrt{2h}\,y\bigr)\,(P\otimes\gamma)(da,dy),\]

because \(\mathcal L(w,x)\otimes\gamma\) is the image of \(P\otimes\gamma\) under \((a,y)\mapsto((w(a),x(a)),y)\). The last integrand is integrable by (1), applied on \(\Omega\times H\) with \(P\otimes\gamma\) (the bound \(|w(a)|\le A\) holds for \(P\otimes\gamma\)-almost every \((a,y)\), the first marginal being \(P\)). Setting. Let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(h\in\mathbb R\), \(X_0\) and \(W_0,W_1,\dots\) square-integrable random vectors in \(H\), and \(w\) a measurable real random variable, such that \((w,X_0)\) is independent of the sequence \((W_k)_{k\ge0}\), the \(W_k\) are mutually independent, and each \(W_k\) has law \(\gamma\). The Euler chain is \(X_{k+1}=X_k-h abla U(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,W_k\). For a function \(F:H o\mathbb R\) write \(T(F,X)=\mathbb E[w\,F(X)]\), and let \(\mathcal L\varphi=\Delta\varphi-\langle abla U, abla\varphi angle\).

Claim. (1) For every \(k\), the joint law of \(((w,X_k),W_k)\) is the product of the law of \((w,X_k)\) and \(\gamma\).

(2) Let \(\varphi\in C^2\) with \(|\varphi|\le C\) and \(|\mathcal L\varphi|\le D\), let \(|w|\le A\) almost surely with \(A\ge0\), and let \(\varphi\) satisfy (1) of Step 1 with \(\varepsilon>0\), \(K\ge0\). Then for \(0\le h\le1\) and every \(k\),

\[ igl|T(\varphi,X_{k+1})-T(\varphi,X_k)-h\,T(\mathcal L\varphi,X_k) igr|\le A\,h\,(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h) igl(1+\| abla U(X_k)\|_{L_2}^2 igr).\]

Proof. (1) Consider the augmented chain \(Z_k=(w,X_k)\) with values in \(\mathbb R imes H\). It satisfies \(Z_{k+1}=\Phi(Z_k,W_k)\) with \(\Phi((s,u),y)=(s,\,u-h abla U(u)+\sqrt{2h}y)\), a measurable map, since the first coordinate is carried along unchanged. For a chain driven by independent noise with common law \(\gamma\) and an initial state independent of the noise, \(Z_k\) is a measurable function of \(Z_0,W_0,\dots,W_{k-1}\), which are independent of \(W_k\); hence the joint law of \((Z_k,W_k)\) is the product of the law of \(Z_k\) and \(\gamma\) (this is proved in the section on independent Euler steps). (2) Apply (3) of Step 1 with \(x=X_k\), \(z=W_k\) and \(b=- abla U\). steps.title: Summing the residuals over a time horizon
steps.body:
Claim. (1) Let \((a_k)\) and \((c_k)\) be real sequences, \(h\in\mathbb R\), \(E\ge0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\). If \(|a_{k+1}-a_k-hc_k|\le E\) for every \(k<n\), then

\[\Bigl|a_n-a_0-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}h\,c_k\Bigr|\le nE.\]

(2) In the setting of Step 2 (2), let \(R\ge0\) with \(\|\nabla U(X_k)\|_{L_2}\le R\) for every \(k\le n\). Then

\[\Bigl|T(\varphi,X_n)-T(\varphi,X_0)-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}h\,T(\mathcal L\varphi,X_k)\Bigr|\le A\,(nh)\,(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h)\,(1+R^2).\]

Proof. (1) The sum telescopes: \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(a_{k+1}-a_k-hc_k)=a_n-a_0-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}hc_k\). By the triangle inequality for finite sums,

\[\Bigl|a_n-a_0-\sum_{k<n}hc_k\Bigr|\le\sum_{k<n}|a_{k+1}-a_k-hc_k|\le\sum_{k<n}E=nE.\]

(2) For \(k<n\) we have \(\|\nabla U(X_k)\|_{L_2}^2\le R^2\), so by Step 2 (2) each local residual is at most \(E=Ah(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h)(1+R^2)\), which is nonnegative. Part (1) with \(a_k=T(\varphi,X_k)\) and \(c_k=T(\mathcal L\varphi,X_k)\) gives the bound \(nE=A(nh)(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h)(1+R^2)\). \(\square\)

In the Dynkin identity, \(nh\) is the fixed time horizon \(t\), and the right-hand side tends to \(At\,\varepsilon(1+R^2)\) as \(h\to0\); since \(\varepsilon>0\) is arbitrary, the Euler sums approximate \(\int_0^tT(\mathcal L\varphi,\cdot)\,ds\).

The observation is the actual probability integral \(E\)[\(w\) \(F(X)]\). Its continuity is proved from boundedness and a second-moment tail estimate, allowing weak Euler limits to be taken on the \(L^{2}\) state space.

\[\mathcal O_{w,F}(X)=\int w(a)F(X(a))\,P(da).\]

AverageLMC/LaplacianWeightClipping.lean.title: Bounded radial weights approximate every square-integrable initial vector
AverageLMC/LaplacianWeightClipping.lean.summary:
The initial coupling error in the Laplacian proof is only square integrable. This module constructs bounded radial clippings whose \(L^{2}\) norms never exceed the original norm. Their pairings converge against every fixed \(L^{2}\) vector by dominated convergence, allowing the later compact-test argument to use bounded scalar weights without adding boundedness to the main theorem hypotheses.

The measurable radial clipping has \(c_n(0)=0\); for \(x\ne0\) it uses radius \(n+1\):

\[c_n(x)=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{n+1}{\|x\|}\right\}x, \qquad\|c_n(x)\|\le\min\{\|x\|,n+1\}.\]

Clipping never increases the actual \(L^2\) norm and converges against every square-integrable vector:

\[\|c_n(\Psi)\|_{L^2(P)}\le\|\Psi\|_{L^2(P)},\qquad \langle c_n(\Psi),D\rangle_{L^2(P)} \longrightarrow\langle\Psi,D\rangle_{L^2(P)}.\]

It is also at most \(n+1\): at a nonzero vector cancel the positive norm against the radial quotient, and handle the zero vector directly. These two bounds serve different purposes: the radius makes every coordinate a bounded test weight, while domination by the original vector supplies the integrable majorant and preserves the sharp final \(L^{2}\) norm.
